title: The purpose of issue management
blurb: Explain why projects manage issues: to resolve the problems that occur, not to stop them happening.
question: A colleague says the purpose of issue management is to stop issues from occurring on the project. Another says it is to address and resolve the issues that do occur. Who is right, and what would you say to the other?

teach.h: Resolve what occurs, keep the project on track
teach.body: The purpose of issue management is to address and resolve the issues that occur, so that their impact on the project's objectives is kept to a minimum and the project stays on track. In plain English: things will go wrong; issue management makes sure that when they do, they are caught, owned, escalated and fixed quickly, with the right person making the call.

teach.h: What issue management is for, and what it is not for

teach.caption: The two work together: good risk management can mean fewer issues, but it can't promise none.

steps.label: Capture
steps.sub: Log the issue and give it an owner

steps.label: Assess
steps.sub: Work out the impact on objectives

steps.label: Resolve
steps.sub: Agree and carry out the fix

teach.caption: The detailed stages of the resolution process are covered in the next lesson.

teach.h: Worked scenario: City Museum app launch
teach.body: Two weeks before launch, the museum's payment provider withdraws its service. The project manager logs it, owns it, and assesses that finding a new provider will take four weeks: well past the one-week tolerance. Within a day she takes it to the sponsor with three options. The sponsor agrees to switch provider and launch a week late with free entry for members. The issue is tracked to closure. Disruption is contained; objectives are protected.

With no issue log and no escalation route, problems sit in inboxes with no owner. Nobody assesses the knock-on effect, so the sponsor hears late, when the cheap options have gone. Similar problems are handled differently each time, and nothing is learned. Issue management replaces that drift with a consistent, visible way of dealing with problems.

teach.text: The classic wrong answer: 'to stop issues occurring'. Issue management can't do that: issues are problems that have already happened. Preventing problems is the proactive job of risk management. Also beware 'to address and resolve uncertainty': uncertainty means risk, not issues.

teach.body: To address and resolve the issues that occur, minimising their impact on objectives and keeping the project on track.

items: Purpose: address and resolve issues that occur, minimise their impact, keep the project on track.
It is responsive: it deals with problems that have happened.
It does NOT stop issues occurring: preventing problems is closer to risk management.
It works by capturing, assessing, escalating, resolving and tracking issues, with the sponsor deciding.

summary: You can now state the purpose of issue management and explain how it differs from risk management. You can also reject the classic distractor that it exists to stop issues happening.

A.q: What is the purpose of issue management?
options: To stop problems from occurring on the project
To resolve problems that occur and limit impact
To reduce the uncertainty in project estimates
To score problems by probability and impact
A.why: Issue management exists to address and resolve the issues that occur, minimising their impact on objectives.

whyNot.0: Issues have already happened, so issue management can't stop them occurring.
whyNot.2: Reducing uncertainty is part of risk management and estimating.
whyNot.3: Probability belongs to risks; issues have already occurred.

A.q: Issue management is best described as being:
options: focused on resolving current problems
focused on preventing future problems
focused on scoring uncertain events
focused on approving scope changes
A.why: Issue management deals with problems that have happened and need resolving now.

whyNot.1: Preventing future problems is the proactive work of risk management.
whyNot.2: Scoring uncertain events is risk analysis.
whyNot.3: Approving scope changes is the job of change control.

A.q: Which outcome shows that issue management is working well?
options: No issues arise at any point in the project
Every problem is passed straight to the sponsor
Issues are resolved before they damage objectives
Risks are removed so issues can no longer occur
A.why: Success is issues caught and resolved quickly, so their impact on objectives is minimised.

whyNot.0: Issues will still arise; managing them well doesn't prevent them.
whyNot.1: Only problems beyond the PM's tolerance go to the sponsor.
whyNot.3: No process removes all risk, and issues can arise from unforeseen events.

B.q:
Which TWO statements describe the purpose of issue management?
1. Minimising the impact of issues on objectives.
2. Preventing issues from ever occurring.
3. Keeping the project on track when problems arise.
4. Identifying opportunities to exploit.
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Issue management resolves issues that occur so their impact is minimised and the project stays on track.

whyNot.0: Statement 2 is wrong: issue management can't stop issues occurring.
whyNot.2: Prevention and opportunity-hunting both belong to risk management.
whyNot.3: Exploiting opportunities is a risk response, not issue management.

B.q: A project has no issue log and no escalation route. What is the most likely result?
options: Risks are scored too cautiously by the team
The sponsor must approve too many changes
Benefits are realised sooner than planned
Problems go unowned and are decided too late
B.why: Without issue management, problems drift without owners and reach the sponsor late, when options are fewer.

whyNot.0: Risk scoring is part of risk analysis and is unaffected by the lack of an issue log.
whyNot.1: A missing escalation route means fewer decisions reach the sponsor, not more.
whyNot.2: Unmanaged problems threaten benefits; they don't speed them up.

B.q: Which activity belongs to issue management rather than risk management?
options: Brainstorming threats
Escalating a breach
Scoring probability
Enhancing a gain
B.why: Escalating a problem that breaches tolerance to the sponsor is a core issue management activity.

whyNot.3: Enhancing an opportunity is a risk response.

C.q: Two weeks before launch, a museum's payment provider withdraws its service. The project manager logs it and asks the sponsor to agree a new provider. What is this achieving?
options: Resolving a problem so objectives are protected
Preventing the problem from happening at all
Transferring the risk to a third-party supplier
Reducing the probability of a future threat
C.why: This is issue management in action: a problem that has occurred is resolved with the sponsor to protect the launch.

whyNot.1: The withdrawal has already happened, so it can't be prevented.
whyNot.2: Transfer is a response to an uncertain threat; this is a current problem.
whyNot.3: There is no probability to reduce: the event has occurred.

C.q: A team member says: 'We do risk management, so we won't need issue management.' Why is this wrong?
options: Issue management is required by law on projects
Risk management deals only with opportunities
Risk management can't stop every problem occurring
Issue management replaces risk management later
C.why: Risk management reduces threats but can't remove them all, and some problems are unforeseen, so issues still need managing.

whyNot.0: It's not a legal requirement; it's needed because problems still happen.
whyNot.1: Risk management covers threats as well as opportunities.
whyNot.3: The two run side by side throughout the project; neither replaces the other.

C.q: Which statement about risk management and issue management is correct?
options: Good issue management means risks never occur
Issue management is one stage of risk analysis
Both share a single register for all entries
Good risk management can mean fewer issues
C.why: Dealing with threats proactively means fewer of them turn into problems, though some issues will still arise.

whyNot.0: Issue management deals with problems after they occur; it has no effect on whether risks occur.
whyNot.1: Issue management is a separate process, not part of risk analysis.
whyNot.2: Risks are recorded in the risk register and issues in the issue log.

reteach.title: The fire brigade and the fire inspector
reteach.question: A town has fire inspectors who check buildings to stop fires starting, and a fire brigade that puts out the fires that still happen. Which one is issue management?

blocks.body: The fire inspector works before anything happens, cutting the chance of a fire: that is risk management. The fire brigade can't stop fires starting; its purpose is to respond to the ones that do, fast, and limit the damage: that is issue management. A town with brilliant inspectors still needs a brigade, because some fires will start anyway.

blocks.text: Asking issue management to stop issues happening is like asking the fire brigade to stop fires starting. That is not its job.

explain.body: Issue management exists to address and resolve the issues that occur, so their impact on objectives is minimised and the project stays on track.

test.q: Complete the statement: issue management exists to ______ the issues that occur.
options: predict and avoid
score and rank
address and resolve
accept and tolerate
test.why: Its purpose is to address and resolve the issues that occur.

whyNot.0: Predicting and avoiding is the proactive work of risk management.
whyNot.1: Scoring and ranking belongs to risk analysis.
whyNot.3: Accepting is a risk response; an issue needs resolving.

explain.body: Issue management can't stop issues occurring: by the time something is an issue, it has happened. Prevention is the proactive job of risk management.

test.q: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of issue management?
options: Keeping the project on track
Limiting the impact of issues
Getting timely decisions made
Stopping issues from occurring
test.why: Issue management responds to issues that have occurred; it cannot stop them happening.

whyNot.0: Keeping the project on track is central to its purpose.
whyNot.1: Minimising impact on objectives is its core aim.
whyNot.2: Timely sponsor decisions are how issues get resolved.

explain.body: Every logged issue gets a named owner, so it is clear who is progressing it. Without an owner, issues drift and nobody chases the fix.

test.q: Why does issue management give every logged issue a named owner?
options: So the sponsor no longer needs to hear of it
So someone is clearly responsible for progress
So its probability can be scored by one person
So it can be closed without any further action
test.why: A named owner makes responsibility for progressing the issue unambiguous.

whyNot.0: Issues beyond tolerance still go to the sponsor.
whyNot.2: Issues have no probability: they have already happened.
whyNot.3: Ownership is about getting it resolved, not closing it early.

explain.body: A clear escalation route brings problems beyond the PM's tolerance to the sponsor quickly, with the facts and options, while there is still time to choose the best fix.

test.q: How does issue management help the project sponsor?
options: It brings them decisions beyond tolerance in time
It removes the need for decision gates entirely
It hands them ownership of the risk register
It lets them delegate the business case to the PM
test.why: Escalation brings the right problems to the sponsor promptly, with the facts needed to decide.

whyNot.1: Decision gates are part of governance and still happen.
whyNot.2: The risk register is normally maintained by the project manager.
whyNot.3: The sponsor owns the business case; issue management doesn't change that.
